title: Computational framework for quantum state tomography of spin ensembles
abstract: We present Tomography-NMR, an open-source Python package that reconstructs quantum density matrices from spectroscopic measurement data. The package implements a complete analysis pipeline for two-qubit quantum state tomography based on the product operator formalism: raw time-domain signals are Fourier-transformed into frequency-domain spectra, spectral peak intensities are mapped to expansion coefficients of the density matrix, and the full quantum state is reconstructed. Three integration methods are provided for different use cases: direct peak height measurement and fixed-parameter numerical integration require no theoretical reference and are suited to unknown states, achieving fidelities of approximately 98\% on a benchmark set of known states, while a systematic parameter optimization against a known target state achieves reconstruction fidelities exceeding 99\% for the same benchmark states. While the detailed theoretical framework for quantum state tomography is well established, the practical procedures for extracting density matrices from experimental spectra are often inadequately documented in the literature and obscured within proprietary software. This package addresses that gap by providing a fully transparent, reproducible implementation of every analysis step, from spectral preprocessing to density matrix visualization. The software has been validated on experimentally prepared two-qubit states measured via nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy of coupled $^{31}$P nuclei. Average reconstruction fidelities range from 0.975 to 0.995 across a benchmark set of 20 two-qubit states, including the computational basis states, Bell states, and the outputs of three fundamental quantum gates (CNOT, H, and T). Although developed for NMR, the modular architecture facilitates adaptation to other spectroscopic platforms and alternative measurement protocols.
summary: This paper introduces Tomography-NMR, an open-source Python package designed to reconstruct quantum density matrices from raw NMR spectroscopic data. It details a complete analysis pipeline that transforms time-domain signals into spectral coefficients using the product operator formalism. The tool achieves high reconstruction fidelities for two-qubit systems, providing a transparent and reproducible methodology for quantum state characterization.
main_problem: The primary challenge is bridging the gap between established quantum state tomography theory and the practical, transparent extraction of density matrices from raw spectroscopic measurement data.
main_result: The authors developed Tomography-NMR, an open-source Python package that achieves high reconstruction fidelities (up to 99.5%) for two-qubit states measured via NMR.
method: The package implements a full pipeline: Fourier transforming time-domain NMR signals to frequency spectra, mapping peak intensities to product operator expansion coefficients, and using three integration methods to reconstruct the density matrix.
model_or_system: The system is a two-qubit spin ensemble, experimentally realized using Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy of coupled protons ($^{31}	ext{P}$). The state is reconstructed using the product operator formalism.
key_observables: Density matrix ($ho$), spectral peak intensities, and reconstruction fidelity (quantified by Fortunato's metric).
important_parameters: The system is currently limited to two qubits; extension to higher qubits requires developing spectral deconvolution methods.
main_assumptions: The method assumes the ability to measure a tomographically complete set of spectral observables, and the optimized routine can be computationally intensive.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the characteristic doublet structure in Q1 and Q2 readout spectra and compare the resulting density matrices reconstructed using the three different integration methods.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the Tomography-NMR package, details the product operator formalism for two-qubit states, describes the three distinct data processing pipelines (peak height, fixed integration, optimized grid search), and validates the results on a benchmark set of 20 states.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial, reproducible, and open-source tool for characterizing quantum states experimentally, which is vital for validating theoretical models in quantum information science.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Minimal set of 9 spectra sufficient to determine all 15 non-identity expansion coefficients of the two-qubit density matrix. Each spectrum displays a doublet with peaks labeled L (left) and R (right). The sum (L+R) and difference (L−R) of peak intensities, extracted from both the real and imaginary parts, are mapped to specific product operator coefficients as indicated. Together, these 9 spectra span the complete set of coefficients required for full state reconstruction.
Figure 2: Theoretical density matrix for the |00⟩computational basis state, visualized as a 3D bar chart. The single non-zero diagonal element at |00⟩⟨00| confirms the pure state ˆρ = |00⟩⟨00|.

Figure 3: Q1 readout channel spectra for all 14 tomographic measurements (7 readout pulses × 2 real/imaginary parts). Red vertical lines mark integration centers; orange shaded regions indicate integration windows of width w = 4 Hz. Each spectrum displays the characteristic doublet separated by J ≈22 Hz.

Figure 4: Q2 readout channel spectra for all 14 tomographic measurements, with indepen- dently adjusted frequency offset. The Q2 channel requires a different offset than Q1 due to slight chemical shift differences between the two 31P nuclei.

Figure 5: Comparison of the density matrix reconstruction from different integration meth- ods. a. Density matrix reconstructed using the peak height method (F = 0.980). While the dominant |00⟩⟨00| element is correctly identified, minor deviations are visible in off- diagonal and subdominant diagonal elements. b. Density matrix from fixed-parameter Simpson integration (F = 0.980). The result is similar to the peak height method, with small differences arising from the noise-averaging effect of finite integration windows. c.
